what: Contact indexer with dwell latch. The red crank carries a retained yellow roller. It enters a slot in the coloured passive wheel, advances it by a quarter turn, then leaves. A second motor moves the orange latch out of the way for engagement and closes it during dwell. Watch the wheel itself as well as both motor badges. A retained roller advances a passive four-slot wheel by quarter turns. A second motor opens and closes the physical latch: compare engagement, dwell and reverse indexing.
try: Select Quartermaster in Examples; its two-motor program loads automatically. Reset to the saved pose, then press Run.
Watch A approach the slot while the latch stays closed. B opens to −45° before A pushes the wheel through its indexing interval, then B closes again.
Count four forward quarter turns and four reverse quarter turns. The wheel returns to its first station after each full group. Its movement is intermittent even while A travels between stations.
During each pause, compare the wheel with the frame. The physical latch retains its station; the program does not command the wheel angle.

For inspection, enable motor override and use small jogs: A is limited to 0…160° before engagement, B to −45…0°. Use the complete program for coordinated indexing; turn override off and reset afterwards.
why: The crank roller can transmit force only while touching a slot wall. Each slot is radial to the wheel shaft, so the contact converts part of the input circle into output rotation. Four equally spaced slots provide four wheel stations. The independently driven latch clears the slot assembly during engagement and restrains it during the remaining input travel. Reversing the coordinated sequence reverses the index direction.
matters: Indexing mechanisms separate transfer motion from a stationary working interval. They are useful when a workpiece must move to a station, settle and remain still for another operation. This model exposes the separate roles of the driver, passive output and dwell latch. Motor arrival alone cannot demonstrate successful transport or retained dwell.
question: If A completes a revolution, must the wheel have advanced exactly one station? What would you expect if the driver roller or the latch were removed?
answer: The input encoder measures the crank, so completing its target proves only that the input moved. With the roller assembly removed, the motors can still finish the sequence while the passive wheel remains at its first station. With the latch removed, contact can still advance the wheel, but station overshoot and drift grow. Observe the wheel independently: a successful run needs eight measured quarter-turn stations, small held drift and a return to the original position. The supplied experiment opens and closes B at specific A phases; arbitrary independent motor commands do not provide that coordination.
further: Compare Stepworks: identify which part transports the output and which retains it between transfers.
Compare continuous gearing with this intermittent output. A ratio inferred only from final turns misses the long stationary intervals and the changing speed during contact.
Use the construction pages to find the retained roller axle, the four radial slots, the passive output shaft and the latch mounting. Which contacts transmit force at each stage?
Measure the wheel angle during each latched pause, using the frame as reference. Repeating the experiment tests station consistency, not hardware accuracy.
formula: Four slots: one index ≈90°; four indexes ≈360°. Crank radius 80 LDU=32 mm; shaft offset (80,80) LDU. Output moves only through contact. A: four forward and four reverse turns; B: 0° closed, −45° open.
